analysis.one_liner: Keeps the coal production fee that pays to clean up abandoned mines through 2036 and lets states and tribes run emergency mine cleanups.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House committee unanimously approved the abandoned-mine cleanup bill, but it never received a vote in the full House before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill extends a fee charged on coal production, which funds the cleanup of abandoned coal mines, for 15 more years. It lets the Interior Department delegate emergency cleanup work at dangerous old mine sites to states and tribal governments, raises the minimum annual grant for states and tribes with approved cleanup programs, and repays money that was withheld from those programs under 2011 budget cuts. The bill cleared a House committee by voice vote in 2021 and was placed on the House's calendar of ready bills in November 2022, but the full House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near abandoned coal mines, where highwalls, mine subsidence, open shafts, and polluted water threaten safety and property. States and tribal governments that run reclamation programs gain faster emergency response, larger guaranteed minimum grants, and repayment of funds withheld during the 2013-2021 budget cuts.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the fee on coal production that fills the Abandoned Mine Reclamation Fund through fiscal year 2036, so cleanup work at abandoned mine sites does not run out of money. [S2] [S4]

Allows the Interior Department to reimburse states and tribal governments for emergency restoration, reclamation, and prevention of the harmful effects of old coal mining, speeding response when a site becomes dangerous. [S2] [S3]
Raises the minimum annual award to states and Indian tribes with approved abandoned mine reclamation programs from $3 million to $5 million. [S2] [S3]

Requires Interior to distribute back to states and tribes, in fiscal 2022, an amount equal to the funds withheld from these programs by 2011 budget-control sequestration between 2013 and 2021, and exempts these payments from future automatic budget cuts. [S4]

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators pay the production fee for 15 additional years, which is likely passed into coal prices. The federal budget bears the cost of repaying the withheld funds and exempting the program from future sequestration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal operators and the federal budget

drawbacks.text: Extending the production fee through 2036 is a cost to coal operators that is likely passed on in coal prices, borne partly by ratepayers and industrial users of coal. [S4]

Repaying withheld funds and exempting the program from sequestration adds to federal spending outside normal budget discipline, which budget-minded critics of earmarked trust-fund carve-outs would object to. [S4]

Delegating emergency reclamation to states and tribes moves decisions about dangerous sites closer to local governments, but it also means the federal emergency program's direct role shrinks; quality and speed would then depend on each state or tribal program's capacity. [S4]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and local: money and authority to fix dangerous abandoned mine sites in coal communities, with an industry fee rather than general taxes as the main funding source. The costs are modest by comparison: a 15-year extension of an existing fee on coal production and a one-time repayment of money previously cut from the program. The main honest objection is the budgeting exception from automatic cuts, not the cleanup itself.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee approved it unanimously and it was placed on the House calendar of ready-to-go bills in November 2022, but the House never voted on it before the term ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 10, 2021 with 11 original cosponsors from both parties, including several Pennsylvania Republicans, and referred to the Natural Resources and Budget Committees. [S6] [S4]
A House subcommittee held a hearing in March 2021, the subcommittee was discharged in May 2021, and the full committee ordered the bill reported by voice vote on May 26, 2021. [S6]

The committee did not formally report the bill until November 16, 2022, the day before the House's final work period before the term's end; the Budget Committee was discharged the same day and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills ready for House floor action. [S6] [S4]
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023. [S6] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators are better off paying no new fee extension, and nothing changed for the abandoned-mine fund; the states and tribes awaiting emergency-response authority and repaid funds got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators; communities got no cleanup help

for.what_they_did: Held a hearing, ordered the bill reported by voice vote on May 26, 2021, and formally reported it with a written report on November 16, 2022.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start: its 31 cosponsors included 25 Democrats and 6 Republicans, several Pennsylvania Republicans were among the original sponsors, and the committee approved it by voice vote with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill extends the per-ton fee operators pay into the abandoned-mine cleanup fund through 2036, a direct cost likely passed into coal prices. The fee's purpose, cleaning up the legacy damage of past mining, serves the communities around the mines, so the industry's obligation here runs alongside the public's interest.

industries.industry: State and tribal abandoned-mine reclamation programs
industries.note: States and tribes would get emergency-response authority, larger guaranteed minimum grants ($5 million instead of $3 million), and repayment of sequestration cuts. This is government capacity, not a private industry, and its gain is the public's gain.
Communities near abandoned mines, the reason Pennsylvania members of both parties backed the bill, would see dangerous sites addressed faster and with more reliable money.
